title: Updated Report Notes 3: Conceptual Phase Mapping
purpose: Maps each chronological experimental phase to its tests, measured results, and the relevant scientific concepts, theories, or assumptions that the phase supports or challenges.
scientific_position: The experiments demonstrate reproducible QPU-executable split-complex subspace emulation behavior, not proof of new physics, formal QEC replacement, physical pulse compression, or cryptographic security.

phases.phase_summary: Initial construction of a split-complex logical mapping inside ordinary complex Hilbert-space quantum circuits.

tests.what_was_tested: Whether split-complex-style transformations could be represented as two-qubit reversible quantum operators.
tests.result: Functional mapping primitive established: CX -> RY(theta) -> CX.
tests.interpretation: Established the base compiler primitive used throughout the project.
tests.caveat: This is an emulation layer, not physical realization of split-complex particles.

conceptual_links.concept: Split-complex logic is only mathematical and not executable on physical quantum hardware.
conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: Split-complex-inspired mappings were executed reproducibly on IBM superconducting hardware with high recovery fidelity.
conceptual_links.what_is_not_yet_proven: This does not establish physical split-complex particles or nonstandard quantum mechanics.
conceptual_links.apa7_reference: Khrennikov, A. (2003). Hyperbolic quantum mechanics. Advances in Applied Clifford Algebras, 13(1), 1–9.

phases.phase_summary: First real-QPU tests showing that reversible mapped states could be recovered after transformation.

tests.what_was_tested: Recovery of payload states after reversible scrambling and inverse transformation.
tests.result: High-fidelity recovery observed.
tests.interpretation: Demonstrated that the mapped architecture could execute on real superconducting hardware.
tests.caveat: Exact backend and post-transpile audit should be recorded for each run.

tests.result: Payload recovered with high fidelity.
tests.interpretation: Supported the claim that the architecture can perform stable reversible payload recovery.

phases.phase_summary: Discovery that the Qiskit transpiler aggressively compresses reversible structures and that compiler behavior is part of the architecture.

tests.what_was_tested: Comparison of structured reversible mapping against an unstructured baseline under repeated transformation loops.
tests.result: Structured mapping retained 99.0% fidelity while baseline showed 63.0%.
tests.interpretation: Showed favorable compiler simplification and recovery stability for the structured mapping.
tests.caveat: Should be described as transpiler-level reduction unless pulse schedules verify physical compression.

conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: Information behaved like recoverable subsystem-style encoding under corruption.
conceptual_links.what_is_not_yet_proven: Formal operator-algebra code-distance scaling has not yet been measured.
conceptual_links.apa7_reference: Kribs, D. W., Laflamme, R., Poulin, D., & Lesosky, M. (2005). Operator quantum error correction. Quantum Information & Computation, 6(4), 382–399.

conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: The mapped subspace showed unusually stable recovery under several noise and sabotage conditions.
conceptual_links.what_is_not_yet_proven: Controlled noise-channel characterization has not yet been completed.
conceptual_links.apa7_reference: Lidar, D. A., Chuang, I. L., & Whaley, K. B. (1998). Decoherence-free subspaces for quantum computation. Physical Review Letters, 81(12), 2594–2597.

phases.phase_summary: Adversarial compiler-resistance test forcing nontrivial physical execution.

tests.what_was_tested: Whether randomized basis switching and phase perturbations could prevent full symbolic cancellation.
tests.result: Native operations survived transpilation: rz=22, sx=20, cz=4, measure=2, barrier=1; compiled depth=29; circuit size=48.
tests.interpretation: The compiler could not erase the adversarial logic entirely, supporting nontrivial hardware execution.
tests.caveat: Still requires statevector and noise-model comparison for physical interpretation.

conceptual_links.concept: Deep reversible circuits necessarily collapse rapidly on NISQ devices.
conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: 97.8% fidelity remained at 100,000 programmed gate-pair depth.
conceptual_links.what_is_not_yet_proven: Physical pulse depth and scheduled-duration immunity have not been established.
conceptual_links.apa7_reference: Preskill, J. (2018). Quantum computing in the NISQ era and beyond. Quantum, 2, 79.

phases.phase_summary: Stress-to-failure test scaling nominal programmed depth to extreme forward/reverse gate-pair counts.

tests.what_was_tested: Forward and inverse split-complex chains at 1,000, 10,000, and 100,000 programmed gate-pair depths.
tests.result: Fidelity remained high across all programmed depths.
tests.interpretation: Nominal programmed depth did not materially degrade recovery in this reversible compiled workload.
tests.caveat: Must log post-transpile physical depth, native gate counts, and scheduled duration before claiming physical depth immunity.

tests.what_was_tested: Two-qubit holographic-style scrambling, shockwave inversion, and target-state reconstruction.
tests.result: Stable recovery after reversible scrambling.
tests.interpretation: Showed stable nonlocal-style recovery behavior in ordinary quantum circuits.
tests.caveat: Does not claim physical wormholes or gravitational spacetime.

conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: Local damage and scrambling still allowed nonlocal recovery of the logical payload.

tests.result: Physical containment survived anti-cancellation design.
tests.interpretation: Recovery remained strong even when the compiler was forced to retain nontrivial native operations.

tests.what_was_tested: Mid-circuit measurement branching designed to defeat trivial compiler cancellation.
tests.result: Runtime control-flow circuit recovered payload above random baseline.
tests.interpretation: One of the hardest tests; demonstrated survivable dynamic control flow.

phases.phase_name: Crowning Discovery: Quantum Embedded Logic Units
phases.phase_summary: Transition from abstract recovery demonstrations into active low-width embedded computation.

tests.what_was_tested: 4-bit input word encoded across 12 physical qubits with sabotage injection and Toffoli-based correction.
tests.result: Original word recovered above random baseline after active sabotage.
tests.interpretation: Demonstrated a low-width embedded logic architecture survivable under NISQ fault conditions.
tests.caveat: Does not prove scalable universal fault-tolerant quantum computing.

conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: Information behaved like recoverable subsystem-style encoding under corruption.

conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: Belnap-style contradiction-tolerant logical structures were represented and recovered on real QPUs.
conceptual_links.what_is_not_yet_proven: No large-scale computational advantage has yet been demonstrated.
conceptual_links.apa7_reference: Belnap, N. D. (1977). A useful four-valued logic. In Modern uses of multiple-valued logic (pp. 8–37). Springer.

tests.what_was_tested: Word-width scaling and QEC-bus containment under active sabotage.
tests.result: 4-bit / 6-bit region identified as practical NISQ sweet spot.
tests.interpretation: Located useful low-width operational regime before coherence wall effects dominate.
tests.caveat: Higher widths degraded sharply on current NISQ hardware.

conceptual_links.experimental_evidence: Information behaved like recoverable subsystem-style encoding under corruption.

phases.phase_summary: Grid search over classical computing word widths to identify NISQ width limits and shunting workaround.

tests.what_was_tested: Fault-tolerant logic scaling across classical word widths.
tests.result: 6-bit / 4-bit QEC bus was usable; 16-bit and 32-bit widths hit NISQ coherence wall.
tests.score: 79.7% boundary core; 77.1% 4-bit QEC bus; 13.3% at 16-bit; 1.4% at 32-bit
tests.interpretation: Mapped the practical width boundary and motivated asynchronous subspace shunting.
tests.caveat: Shunting is architectural emulation, not proof that a physical 156-qubit device executed a full 192-track machine natively.

phases.phase_summary: Model-separation test comparing split-complex mapped operator against standard RZ phase baseline.

tests.what_was_tested: 78 circuits across 13 theta angles and X/Y/Z bases with anti-cancellation perturbations.
tests.result: Large model separation between standard RZ baseline and split-complex mapped operator.
tests.interpretation: Confirmed that the mapped operator is not behaviorally equivalent to a simple complex RZ phase baseline.
tests.caveat: This is not yet a standard quantum mechanics violation; next step is same-circuit hardware-vs-statevector residual analysis.
